syntax of Zhon_adve

description::
=== _syntaxZhon: Subject + Adverb + Verb + Object:
· _sntxZhon: 我 昨天 吃 肉。 :: _sntxSubj:[Wǒ] _sntxTime:[zuótiān] _sntxVerb:{chī} _sntxObj1:[ròu]. != I [yesterday] eat meat. != I ate meat yesterday.
· _sntxZhon: 我 也 是 美国人。 :: _sntxSubj:[Wǒ] _sntxAddition:[yě] _sntxVerb:{shì} _sntxSbjc:[měiguórén]。 != [I] [also] {am} [American].

=== _syntaxZhon: Adverb + Subject + Verb + Object:
· _sntxZhon: 今天经理有会。 :: _sntxTime:[Jīntiān] _sntxSubj:[jīnglǐ] _sntxVerb:{yǒu} _sntxSbjc:[huì]. != The manager has a meeting today.

=== _syntaxZhon: Adverb Adverb Verb:
· _sntxZhon: 我们 常常 一起 散步。 :: _sntxSubj:[Wǒmen] _sntxTime:[chángcháng] _sntxManner:[yīqǐ] _sntxVerb:{sànbù}. != We frequently take walks together.
=== _syntaxZhon: Adjective + (地-de) + Verb:
· _sntxZhon: 你 要 努力 地 学习。 :: _sntxSubj:[Nǐ] _sntxVerb:{yào} _sntxObj1:[_sntxOther:[nǔlì (de)] _sntxVerb:{xuéxí}]. != You must study hard.
· "You can easily convert most Chinese adjectives into adverbs with the particle 地 (de)."
[{2023-08-07 retrieved} https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/Turning_adjectives_into_adverbs]

=== _syntaxZhon: Adjective + Adverb + (了-le):
· _sntxZhon: 我 累 死了。 :: _sntxSubj:[Wǒ] _sntxSbjc:[[lěi] [sǐ le]]. != I’m so tired.
· _sntxZhon: 这个 主意 好 极了 。 :: _sntxSubj:[Zhège zhǔyi] _sntxSbjc:[hǎo jíle]. != This idea is perfect.

=== _syntaxZhon: Noun Adverb:
· _sntxZhon: 我们 都 是 学生。 :: _sntxSubj:[Wǒmen dōu] _sntxVerb:{shì} _sntxSbjc:[xuéshēng]. != We are **all** students.

=== _syntaxZhon: time:
· "Time words can appear in one of two positions in the sentence in Chinese: either at the beginning of the sentence (before the subject), or directly after the subject."
[{2023-06-21 retrieved} https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/Time_words_and_word_order]

Zhon_adve.SPECIFIC

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2025-11-01}
"· give me a big list of Chinese adverbs with example sentences:
Of course! This is a fantastic way to build fluency. Chinese adverbs are essential for adding nuance, tone, and detail to your sentences.
Here is a substantial list of common and useful Chinese adverbs, categorized by function, with Pinyin and example sentences.
---
### 1. Adverbs of Degree (描述程度)
These answer the question "To what degree?"
* **很 (hěn)** - very, quite
· example: 这本书**很**有趣。 != This book is **very** interesting.
* **非常 (fēicháng)** - extremely, very
· example: 我**非常**感谢你的帮助。 != I am **extremely** grateful for your help.
* **太 (tài)** - too (excessively); (in exclamations) so
· example: 这件衣服**太**贵了。 != This piece of clothing is **too** expensive.
· example: 你**太**好了！ != You are **so** kind!
* **最 (zuì)** - the most
· example: 春天是我**最**喜欢的季节。 != Spring is my **most** favorite season.
* **更 (gèng)** - even more
· example: 我想找一个**更**好的工作。 != I want to find an **even better** job.
* **特别 (tèbié)** - especially, particularly
· example: 我**特别**喜欢中国的美食。 != I **especially** like Chinese food.
* **有点(儿) (yǒudiǎn(r))** - a little bit, somewhat (often for negative things)
· example: 我今天**有点**累。 != I'm **a little bit** tired today.
* **几乎 (jīhū)** - almost, nearly
· example: 我**几乎**每天都去健身房。 != I go to the gym **almost** every day.
* **挺 (tǐng)** - quite, rather (colloquial)
· example: 这个电影**挺**好看的。 != This movie is **quite** good.
* **极其 (jíqí)** - extremely, exceedingly (formal)
· example: 这是一个**极其**重要的任务。 != This is an **extremely** important mission.
---
### 2. Adverbs of Scope (描述范围)
These answer the question "Who or what is included?"
* **都 (dōu)** - all, both
· example: 我们**都**是学生。 != We are **all** students.
* **只 (zhǐ)** / **只是 (zhǐshì)** - only, just
· example: 我**只**喝咖啡，不喝茶。 != I **only** drink coffee, not tea.
* **一共 (yīgòng)** / **总共 (zǒnggòng)** - in total, altogether
· example: 我们班**一共**有二十个学生。 != Our class has twenty students **in total**.
* **一起 (yīqǐ)** - together
· example: 我们**一起**学习中文吧。 != Let's study Chinese **together**.
* **光 (guāng)** - solely, only (emphasizing exclusivity)
· example: **光**说不做是没有用的。 != **Just** talking without doing is useless.
---
### 3. Adverbs of Time (描述时间)
These answer the question "When? How often?"
* **已经 (yǐjīng)** - already
· example: 他**已经**回家了。 != He has **already** gone home.
* **才 (cái)** - not until, only then (indicates something happened later than expected)
· example: 他晚上十一点**才**睡觉。 != He didn't go to bed **until** 11 pm.
* **就 (jiù)** - then, right away (indicates something happened sooner than expected)
· example: 我明天**就**回来。 != I will come back **right away** tomorrow.
* **经常 (jīngcháng)** - often
· example: 我**经常**去那儿吃饭。 != I **often** go there to eat.
* **总是 (zǒngshì)** - always
· example: 他**总是**很忙。 != He is **always** busy.
* **有时候 (yǒu shíhou)** - sometimes
· example: 我**有时候**自己做饭。 != I **sometimes** cook for myself.
* **马上 (mǎshàng)** - immediately, right away
· example: 会议**马上**就要开始了。 != The meeting is about to start **immediately**.
* **终于 (zhōngyú)** - finally, at last
· example: 你**终于**来了！ != You're **finally** here!
* **一直 (yīzhí)** - continuously, always
· example: 雨**一直**在下。 != It's been raining **continuously**.
* **从来 (cónglái)** - always (used with 不 or 没 for "never")
· example: 我**从来**没去过北京。 != I have **never** been to Beijing.
---
### 4. Adverbs of Negation (否定副词)
These are used to negate.
* **不 (bù)** - not (for present/future and habitual actions)
· example: 我**不**知道。 != I **don't** know.
* **没 (méi)** - not (for past actions and to indicate "have not")
· example: 我**没**吃早饭。 != I **didn't** eat breakfast.
* **别 (bié)** - don't (used for commands)
· example: **别**忘了！ != **Don't** forget!
* **不必 (bùbì)** - need not
· example: 你**不必**担心。 != You **don't need to** worry.
---
### 5. Adverbs of Mood or Tone (语气副词)
These express the speaker's attitude or mood.
* **当然 (dāngrán)** - of course
· example: — 你会来吗？ — **当然**！ != — Will you come? — **Of course**!
* **居然 (jūrán)** - unexpectedly, to one's surprise
· example: 他**居然**忘了我的生日。 != He **actually** forgot my birthday.
* **果然 (guǒrán)** - sure enough, as expected
· example: 我说会下雨，**果然**下了。 != I said it would rain, and **sure enough**, it did.
* **其实 (qíshí)** - actually, in fact
· example: 这个问题**其实**很简单。 != This problem is **actually** very simple.
* **大概 (dàgài)** - probably, roughly
· example: 他**大概**三十岁。 != He is **probably** thirty years old.
* **肯定 (kěndìng)** - definitely, certainly
· example: 他**肯定**会同意。 != He will **definitely** agree.
* **也许 (yěxǔ)** / **或许 (huòxǔ)** - perhaps, maybe
· example: 明天**也许**会下雨。 != It **might** rain tomorrow.
* **根本 (gēnběn)** - at all, simply (often used with 不 or 没 for emphasis)
· example: 我**根本**不认识他。 != I don't know him **at all**.
---
### 6. Adverbs of Manner (描述方式)
These answer the question "How?"
* **慢慢地 (mànmàn de)** - slowly
· example: 请**慢慢地**说。 != Please speak **slowly**.
* **小心地 (xiǎoxīn de)** - carefully
· example: 他**小心地**打开了盒子。 != He **carefully** opened the box.
* **一起 (yīqǐ)** - together
· example: 我们**一起**去。 != Let's go **together**.
* **亲自 (qīnzì)** - personally, in person
· example: 经理**亲自**来了。 != The manager came **in person**.
* **突然 (tūrán)** - suddenly
· example: 他**突然**站了起来。 != He stood up **suddenly**.
### Key Grammar Notes:
1. **Position:** Most adverbs are placed **before the verb or adjective** they modify. For example, 很忙 (hěn máng - very busy), 不说 (bù shuō - not speak).
2. **的 (de):** Adverbs of manner are often formed by adding 地 (de) to an adjective. E.g., 慢 (màn - slow) -> 慢慢地 (mànmàn de - slowly).
3. **都 (dōu):** The adverb 都 (dōu - all) must be placed *after* the subject it refers to. E.g., 我们**都**喜欢 (We all like), not 都我们喜欢.
This list provides a strong foundation. Try to incorporate a few of these into your speaking and writing each day to make your Chinese sound more natural and expressive"
[{2025-11-01 retrieved} https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/7313a363-01d8-48e3-a0fb-ba082dbafb6c]

Zhon_adve.regularNo

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2026-06-11}
"This is an excellent question because, like adjectives and nouns, Chinese adverbs have no morphological irregularities (no conjugation, no comparison). However, there are **syntactic and semantic irregularities** that frequently confuse learners.
In Chinese, adverbs (副词 *fùcí*) generally come before verbs/adjectives and cannot be used alone as predicates. But some adverbs break the "normal" rules.
Below are the main categories of irregular Chinese adverb behavior.
---
## 1. Adverbs that cannot be negated normally
Most adverbs can be negated with 不 (*bù*) placed before them:
不常 (bù cháng – not often), 不一定 (bù yīdìng – not necessarily).
But some **frequency and degree adverbs** reject 不 negation directly.
| Adverb | Pinyin | Meaning | Negated form | Notes |
|--------|--------|---------|--------------|-------|
| 很 | hěn | very | ❌ 不很 (dialectal/rare) | Use 不太 (bù tài) instead |
| 极 | jí | extremely | ❌ 不极 | Use 不很 / 不太 |
| 最 | zuì | most | ❌ 不最 | Use 不是最 + Adj |
| 都 | dōu | all / both | ❌ 不都 (ungrammatical) | Use 不全是 / 并非都 |
| 总 | zǒng | always | ❌ 不总 | Use 不总是 (bù zǒngshì) – note 总是 is the full form |
| 非常 | fēicháng | very / extremely | ❌ 不非常 | Use 不太 / 不那么 |
**Why irregular?** – 不 typically negates the verb/adjective after the adverb, not the adverb itself. These adverbs are **semantically absolute** or structurally bound.
**Correct alternatives:**
- 不很 → 不太美 (not very beautiful)
- 不最 → 不是最美的 (not the most beautiful)
- 不都 → 不全是好的 (not all are good)
---
## 2. Adverbs that cannot be used with 了 (le) for completed actions
Most adverbs can appear before 了 (*le*) to indicate completed actions:
他吃了 (tā chī le – he ate).
But **negation adverbs** and **certain time adverbs** reject 了 in the same clause.
| Adverb | Pinyin | Meaning | With 了? | Example | Correct form |
|--------|--------|---------|----------|---------|--------------|
| 不 | bù | not | ❌ 不了 + V | ~~他不了吃~~ | 他没吃 |
| 别 | bié | don't | ❌ 别了 + V | ~~别了去~~ | 别去 |
| 从未 | cóngwèi | never | ❌ 从未了 | ~~他从未了去过~~ | 他从未去过 (no 了) |
| 始终 | shǐzhōng | from start to finish | ❌ 始终了 | ~~他始终了等~~ | 他一直在等 |
**Why irregular?** – 不 and 别 express present/future or general negation, not past completion. For past negation, use 没 (méi) + V + (了) is optional. 从未 implies no completion ever, so 了 is redundant.
**Exception:** 不了 (*bù liǎo*) is a different word meaning "cannot" or "no way" – not 不 + 了.
---
## 3. Adverbs with irregular placement (must follow subject)
Most Chinese adverbs can appear either before or after the subject, depending on scope:
- 今天我很快乐 (Jīntiān wǒ hěn kuàilè) – Today I am happy. ✅
- 我今天很快乐 (Wǒ jīntiān hěn kuàilè) – I today am happy. ✅
But some adverbs **must** come **after** the subject (or topic) and cannot appear sentence-initially.
| Adverb | Pinyin | Meaning | Sentence-initial? | Correct position |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------------|------------------|
| 都 | dōu | all / both | ❌ 都我们去了 | 我们**都**去了 |
| 也 | yě | also / too | ❌ 也他来了 | 他**也**来了 |
| 就 | jiù | then / exactly | ❌ (as adverb) 就他来了? | 他**就**来了 (means "he came right away") |
| 才 | cái | then and only then / just | ❌ 才他走 | 他**才**走 |
| 还 | hái | still / also | ❌ 还她没到 | 她**还**没到 |
| 只 | zhǐ | only | ❌ 只我吃 | 我**只**吃 (but: 只有我吃 "only I eat" – 只有 is different) |
**Why irregular?** – These are **scope adverbs** that must immediately precede the verb or the element they modify, and they cannot float to the front of the sentence except in specific contrastive structures (e.g., 就连...都...).
**Special case:** 都 can appear sentence-initially in fixed patterns like 都说了... (Dōu shuō le... "Everyone said...") but that's colloquial and exceptional.
---
## 4. Adverbs that cannot be modified by degree words
Most adverbs cannot be modified by degree words anyway (you can't say "very often" as 很常常 in Chinese – you just say 常常). But some adverbs **can** take degree modifiers, and some cannot.
| Adverb | Pinyin | Meaning | Can take 很? | Example |
|--------|--------|---------|--------------|---------|
| 常常 | chángcháng | often | ❌ 很常常 | ❌ 他很常常去 |
| 有时 | yǒushí | sometimes | ❌ 很有时 | ❌ 他很有时迟到 |
| 立刻 | lìkè | immediately | ❌ 很立刻 | ❌ 他很立刻反应 |
| 忽然 | hūrán | suddenly | ❌ 很忽然 | ❌ 他很忽然出现 |
| 渐渐 | jiànjiàn | gradually | ❌ 很渐渐 | ❌ 他很渐渐消失 |
Compare with **gradable adverbs** (which are actually adjectives used adverbially):
| Word | As adjective | As adverb with 很 |
|------|--------------|-------------------|
| 快 | kuài – fast | 很快地跑 (runs very fast) ✅ |
| 慢 | màn – slow | 很慢地走 (walks very slowly) ✅ |
| 认真 | rènzhēn – serious | 很认真地学 (studies very seriously) ✅ |
**Why irregular?** – Non-gradable adverbs (frequency, time point, manner that is punctual or absolute) reject degree words. Gradable adverbs are actually adjectives with 地.
---
## 5. Adverbs that change meaning when reduplicated
Most Chinese adverbs do not reduplicate. Some can, but the meaning changes irregularly.
| Base adverb | Pinyin | Meaning | Reduplicated | Meaning |
|-------------|--------|---------|--------------|---------|
| 刚 | gāng | just (a moment ago) | 刚刚 | just now (same meaning, but more colloquial) |
| 常 | cháng | often | 常常 | often (same meaning, more natural) |
| 正 | zhèng | exactly / in progress | 正在 | in progress (same meaning, but 正在 is standard) |
| 好 | hǎo | very / quite | 好好 | properly / well (e.g., 好好学习 – study well) |
**Irregular example:**
好好 does not mean "very very" – it changes to an adverbial meaning "diligently / properly."
| Adverb | Pinyin | Meaning | Reduplicated | Meaning change |
|--------|--------|---------|--------------|----------------|
| 快 | kuài | fast / quickly | 快快 | quickly (no change, but rare) |
| 慢 | màn | slowly | 慢慢 | slowly (no change) |
| 早 | zǎo | early | 早早 | early / ahead of time (e.g., 早早起床) |
**Why irregular?** – Reduplication of monosyllabic adverbs is rare and often lexicalized. The meaning is usually the same or intensified, but 好好 is a clear irregularity.
---
## 6. Negative adverbs with irregular scope (不 vs. 没 vs. 别)
This is the most famous "irregular" area for learners: the three negative adverbs cannot be used interchangeably, and their rules are different from English.
| Negative | Pinyin | Use case | Irregular restriction |
|----------|--------|----------|------------------------|
| 不 | bù | Present/future, general negation, habitual, subjective will | Cannot negate completed actions (use 没) |
| 没 | méi | Past negation, "did not," lack of existence (有) | Cannot be used with future or habitual actions |
| 别 | bié | Negative command ("don't") | Cannot be used in statements (only imperatives / suggestions) |
**Irregular examples:**
| English | Incorrect | Correct | Reason |
|---------|-----------|---------|--------|
| I didn't eat | ~~我不吃~~ (present/habitual) | 我没吃 | Completed action |
| I don't eat meat | ~~我没吃肉~~ (sounds like "didn't eat meat at that meal") | 我不吃肉 | Habitual/general |
| Don't go! | ~~不去！~~ (incomplete) | 别去！ | Imperative |
| Not going | 不去 (statement) | — | No problem |
**Very irregular behavior:** 没 + 有 = 没有 (méiyǒu – there is no / did not have) but 不 + 有 is impossible. Instead, use 没有.
---
## 7. Adverbs that are actually verbs (and thus behave irregularly)
Some words are called "adverbs" in textbooks but function as **modal verbs** or **copulas** syntactically. They can take negation, appear alone as predicates, or take objects – which true adverbs cannot do.
| Word | Pinyin | Textbook "adverb" meaning | Actual syntactic behavior |
|------|--------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| 一定 | yīdìng | certainly / necessarily | Can be predicate: 这是一定的 (This is certain) ✅ |
| 可能 | kěnéng | maybe / possibly | Can take object: 可能下雨 (Maybe it will rain) but also 这不可能 (This is impossible) – acts like adjective/verb |
| 必须 | bìxū | must | Can be negated: 不必 (need not) – behaves like modal verb |
| 应该 | yīnggāi | should | Can be predicate: 这是应该的 (This is how it should be) |
**Test for true adverb:** Cannot be negated with 不 directly before the main verb? No – these can. But they also can appear as main predicate, which adverbs cannot.
**Example of true adverb:** 很 (hěn) – you cannot say ~~这很~~ as a complete sentence meaning "This is very."
---
## Summary Table of Irregular Adverb Behaviors
| Irregularity | Example | Why it's a problem |
|--------------|---------|--------------------|
| Cannot be negated with 不 | ~~不很~~ → 不太 | Most adverbs allow direct negation |
| Cannot appear with 了 | ~~不吃了~~ (as "didn't eat") | Standard negation of past uses 没 |
| Must follow subject | ~~都我们去了~~ → 我们都去了 | Scope adverbs are fixed post-subject |
| Cannot take degree words | ~~很常常~~ | Non-gradable adverbs reject 很 |
| Reduplication changes meaning | 好 → 好好 (properly, not "very very") | Meaning is not predictable |
| Three negative adverbs (不/没/别) non-interchangeable | ~~不去~~ for "didn't go" | Aspect and mood are encoded in negation |
| Behaves like verb (predicate-capable) | 应该 as predicate | True adverbs cannot be main predicate |
---
## Final Note
Chinese adverbs have **no morphological irregularities** whatsoever. All irregularities are:
1. **Collocational** (which adverbs pair with 不, 没, 了, etc.)
2. **Positional** (pre-subject vs. post-subject)
3. **Semantic** (absolute vs. gradable)
4. **Syntactic** (true adverb vs. verb/adjective used adverbially)
The most practically important irregularity for daily use is the **不 vs. 没 vs. 别** system. Master that, and the others are relatively minor exceptions."
[{2026-06-11 retrieved} https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/961747a5-79d0-4647-a94e-a58b10e1c37e]

Zhon_adve.001-ànshí-按时!=on_time::
· time: on time.
· _sntxZhon: 请 按时 交 作业。 :: _sntxArgt:[qǐng] _sntxTime:[ànshí] _sntxVerb:{jiāo} _sntxObj1:[zuòyè] != Please hand in homework on time. !~ note: The sentence has no overt subject, which is standard in Chinese imperatives. The implied subject is the second-person pronoun 你 (nǐ, singular “you”) or 你们 (nǐmen, plural “you”), recoverable from context.

* McsEngl.Zhon_adve.001-ànshí-按时!=on_time,

Zhon_adve.107-huòxǔ-或许!=perhaps::
· mood: perhaps, maybe

Here are example sentences with **或许** (huòxǔ), showing various positions and contexts:
· _sntxZhon: **或许**他今天不会来了。 :: **Huòxǔ** tā jīntiān bù huì lái le. != **Perhaps** he won't come today. |
· _sntxZhon: **或许**你是对的，但我需要再想想。 :: **Huòxǔ** nǐ shì duì de, dàn wǒ xūyào zài xiǎngxiang. != **Maybe** you're right, but I need to think it over. |
· _sntxZhon: 这条路走不通，我们**或许**该试试另一条。 :: Zhè tiáo lù zǒu bù tōng, wǒmen **huòxǔ** gāi shìshi lìng yī tiáo. != This road is blocked; we **might** want to try another one. |
· _sntxZhon: 她**或许**已经知道真相了。 :: Tā **huòxǔ** yǐjīng zhīdào zhēnxiàng le. != She **probably** already knows the truth. |
· _sntxZhon: **或许**有一天，我们会再见面。 :: **Huòxǔ** yǒu yī tiān, wǒmen huì zài jiànmiàn. != **Perhaps** one day, we will meet again. |
· _sntxZhon: 这个问题**或许**比我想象的更复杂。 :: Zhège wèntí **huòxǔ** bǐ wǒ xiǎngxiàng de gèng fùzá. != This problem **may** be more complicated than I imagined. |
· _sntxZhon: 他**或许**不是故意的。 :: Tā **huòxǔ** bù shì gùyì de. != He **might not** have done it on purpose. |
· _sntxZhon: **或许**吧，谁知道呢？ :: **Huòxǔ** ba, shéi zhīdào ne? != **Maybe**, who knows? |
· _sntxZhon: 人生**或许**就是这样，充满了意外。 :: Rénshēng **huòxǔ** jiùshì zhèyàng, chōngmǎn le yìwài. != Life **is perhaps** just like this, full of surprises. |
· _sntxZhon: 你**或许**应该跟他谈谈。 :: Nǐ **huòxǔ** yīnggāi gēn tā tántan. != You **might** want to talk to him. |
---
### Quick Notes
- **Position:** 或许 can go at the **beginning** of a sentence or **before the verb/adjective**.
- **Tone:** Slightly more literary or reflective than 可能 (kěnéng) or 也许 (yěxǔ).
- **Meaning range:** From "perhaps" (uncertain) to "probably" (fairly likely but not certain).

Zhon_adve.079-yílǜ-一律!=without-exception::
· scope.
· _sntxZhon: 迟到者一律罚款。 :: Chídào zhě yīlǜ fákuǎn. != Latecomers will be fined without exception.
· Voice: The clause is in a notional passive construction. 迟到者 is the patient — the person fined — not the agent (the one imposing the fine). The agent is omitted (likely an authority or institution, recoverable from context). No passive marker (被) is needed because:
- The subject is a generic/regulatory class

Zhon_verb_mebr.negative

description::
"The most commonly used negating element is bù (不), pronounced with second tone when followed by a fourth tone. This can be placed before a verb, preposition or adverb to negate it. For example: "I don't eat chicken" (我不吃鸡; 我不吃雞; wǒ bù chī jī; 'I not eat chicken'). For the double-verb negative construction with bù, see Complement of result, below. However, the verb yǒu (有)—which can mean either possession, or "there is/are" in existential clauses—is negated using méi (没; 沒) to produce méiyǒu (没有; 沒有; 'not have').
For negation of a verb intended to denote a completed event, méi or méiyǒu is used instead of bù (不), and the aspect marker le (了) is then omitted. Also, méi[yǒu] is used to negate verbs that take the aspect marker guo (过; 過); in this case the aspect marker is not omitted.[39]
In coverb constructions, the negator may come before the coverb (preposition) or before the full verb, the latter being more emphatic. In constructions with a passive marker, the negator precedes that marker; similarly, in comparative constructions, the negator precedes the bǐ phraseNot clear (unless the verb is further qualified by gèng (更, "even more"), in which case the negator may follow the gèng to produce the meaning "even less").[40]
The negator bié (别) precedes the verb in negative commands and negative requests, such as in phrases meaning "don't ...", "please don't ...".
The negator wèi (未) means "not yet". Other items used as negating elements in certain compound words include wú (无; 無),wù (勿), miǎn (免) and fēi (非).
A double negative makes a positive, as in sentences like wǒ bú shì bù xǐhuān tā (我不是不喜欢她; 我不是不喜歡她, "It's not that I don't like her" )."
[{2021-11-30 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_grammar#Negation]

name::
* McsEngl.Zhon_verb_mebr.negative,
* McsEngl.negative-Zhon_verb_mebr,

Zhon_verb_mebr.imperative

description::
"Second-person imperative sentences are formed in the same way as statements, but like in English, the subject "you" is often omitted.
Orders may be softened by preceding them with an element such as qǐng (请, "to ask"), in this use equivalent to English "please". See Particles for more. The sentence-final particle ba (吧) can be used to form first-person imperatives, equivalent to "let's..."."
[{2021-12-01 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_grammar#Imperatives]

· _sntxZhon: _sntxVerb:{请坐} _sntxSpace:[下]。 Qǐng zuò xià. != {please sit} [down].

name::
* McsEngl.Zhon_verb_mebr.imperative,
* McsEngl.imperative-Zhon_verb_mebr,

Zhon_verb_mebr.reduplicated

description::
"One of the fun things about Chinese is that when speaking, you can repeat a verb to express "a little bit" or "briefly." This is called reduplication. It creates a casual tone, and a sense that whatever the action is, it's not going to take long."
[{2021-10-16 retrieved} https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/Reduplication_of_verbs]

"The delimitative aspect denotes an action that goes on only for some time, "doing something 'a little bit'".[37] This can be expressed by reduplication of a monosyllabic verb, like the verb zǒu (走 "walk") in the following sentence:
· _sntxZhon: 我 到公園 走走。:: _sntxSubj:[wǒ] _sntxSpaceDire:[(dào) gōngyuán] _sntxVerb:{zǒu zǒu} != I to park walk walk != I'm going for a walk in the park.
An alternative construction is reduplication with insertion of "one" (一 yī). For example, zǒu yi zǒu (走一走), which might be translated as "walk a little walk". A further possibility is reduplication followed by kàn (看 "to see"); this emphasizes the "testing" nature of the action. If the verb has an object, kàn follows the object.
Some compound verbs, such as restrictive-resultative and coordinate compounds, can also be reduplicated on the pattern tǎolùn-tǎolùn (讨论讨论; 討論討論), from the verb tǎolùn (讨论; 討論), meaning "discuss". Other compounds may be reduplicated, but for general emphasis rather than delimitative aspect. In compounds that are verb–object combinations, like tiào wǔ (跳舞; 'to jump a dance', "dance"), a delimitative aspect can be marked by reduplicating the first syllable, creating tiào-tiào wǔ (跳跳舞), which may be followed with kàn (看)."
[{2021-12-03 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_grammar#Aspects]

name::
* McsEngl.Zhon_verb_mebr.reduplicated,
* McsEngl.reduplicated-Zhon_verb_mebr,
* McsEngl.Zhon_verb'reduplication,

· _sntxZhon: 小心 啊 ！ Xiǎoxīn a! != Be careful!

Zhon_verb_auxi.bù-不-negation

description::
· bù-不 denotes not.

=== negates present:
· _sntxZhon: 我 今天 晚上 不 喝酒。 :: Wǒ jīntiān wǎnshang bù hējiǔ. != Tonight I'm not going to drink.

=== negates future:
· _sntxZhon: 老板 明天 不 来 。 :: Lǎobǎn míngtiān bù lái. != The boss won't come tomorrow.

=== negates habitual-actions:
· _sntxZhon: 我 不吃 鸡。 :: _sntxSubj:[Wǒ] _sntxVerb:{bù chī} _sntxObj1:[jī]。 != [I] {not eat} [chicken].

=== negates adjectives:
· _sntxZhon: 我 不 饿。 :: _sntxSubj:[Wǒ] _sntxVerb:{bù} _sntxSbjc:[è]. != I'm not hungry.

=== for asking questions: verb bu verb:
· _sntxZhon: 你 是 不是 我 的 老师？ :: _sntxSubj:[Nǐ] _sntxVerb:{shì bu shì} _sntxSbjc:[wǒ de lǎoshī]? != Are you my teacher or not?

=== for tag-questions:
· _sntxZhon: 我们 去 吃饭 ，好 不 好？ :: Wǒmen qù chīfàn, hǎo bu hǎo? != Let's go eat, is that OK?

=== negates specific verbs:
· "Certain verbs just don't get negated by 没 (méi) or 没有 (méiyǒu) ever. These include the verbs 是 (shì) ("to be") and 在 (zài) ("to be (in a place)"), as well as some psychological verbs such as 知道 (zhīdào) ("to know") and 认识 (rènshi) ("to know (a person)"). For these verbs, it's best to just take them on a case-by-case basis. Being aware of their existence can save you a fair bit of confusion."
[{2023-07-09 retrieved} https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/Comparing_%22bu%22_and_%22mei%22]
· _sntxZhon: 昨天 我 不 在 家 。 :: Zuótiān wǒ bù zài jiā. != I was not home yesterday.

* McsEngl.Zhon_verb_auxi.bù-不!=negation,

Zhon_verb_auxi.le-了

description::
=== le-了 denotes completion.
· _sntxZhon: 我回家了。 _sntxSubj:[Wǒ] _sntxVerb:{huí} _sntxObj1:[jiā] {le}。 != [I] {went} [home]. I'm home.
· _sntxZhon: 我走了四十分钟。 _sntxSubj:[Wǒ] _sntxVerb:{zǒu le} _sntxTimeInterval:[sìshí fēnzhōng]。 != [I] {walked} [(for) forty miniutes].
· "The particle 了 (le) has a lot of uses. One of the most common is to express the completion of an action. This is called aspect, which is not the same as tense. Tense is about when an action happens: past, present or future. With regards to 了 (le), aspect is about whether the action is complete in a certain time frame."
[{2023-06-25 retrieved} https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/Expressing_completion_with_%22le%22]

=== already:
· _sntxZhon: 他们 工作 了。 :: _sntxSubj:[Tāmen] _sntxVerb:{gōngzuò le}. != They (already) work. (This expression emphasizes that they're not students anymore, and have already entered the workforce.)

=== now:
· _sntxZhon: 懂 了。 Dǒng le. != Now I understand.

=== with 太-tài-too:
· _sntxZhon: 老师 太 累 了。 :: _sntxSubj:[Lǎoshī] _sntxSbjc:[tài lèi] {le}. != The teacher is too tired.

=== change in state:
· _sntxZhon: 你 胖 了。 :: _sntxSubj:[Nǐ] _sntxSbjc:[pàng] {le}. != You've gotten fat. (You used to not be fat.)
· _sntxZhon: 我 不 买 了。 :: _sntxSubj:[Wǒ] _sntxVerb:{bù mǎi le}. != I'm not buying it now. (I had previously decided to buy it.)
· "了 (le) has many uses. You probably first learned 了 (le) as a particle that tells you an action is completed, which is also known as "了1." However, this article is not about that use of 了 (le); instead, it is about indicating a change of state (了2). In other words, there is now a new situation, or there is about to be a new situation."
[{2023-06-24 retrieved} https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/Change_of_state_with_%22le%22]

description::
· "To show the past tense in Chinese, use 过 after the verb to indicate that the action has happened before. However, there are certain limitations to the verbs that can be used with 过. Verbs of recognition and verbs that only happen once cannot be used with 过.
e.g.
我去过北京。(Wǒ qùguò běijīng.) I have been to Beijing.
你吃过饺子吗？(Nǐ chīguò jiǎozi ma?) Have you ever eaten dumplings?
我们学过这本书。(Wǒmen xuéguò zhè běn shū.) We have studied this book."

Zhon_verb_auxi.zhe-着

description::
"To show the continuation of an action or state in Chinese, 着 is added after the verb. The usual structure is Subject + Verb + 着（+ Object）.
e.g.
门开着。(Mén kāizhe.) The door is open.
地上坐着一只狗。(Dìshàng zuòzhe yī zhī gǒu.) A dog is sitting on the ground.
他穿着一件长袖。(Tā chuān zhe yī jiàn cháng xiù.) He is wearing long sleeves.
When 着 is used with words like 在 or 正在, it indicates the present progressive tense .
e.g.
我正在做着饭，他就来了。(Wǒ zhèngzài zuòzhe fàn, tā jiù láile.) I was cooking when he came.
他在公园里听着歌呢。(Tā zài gōngyuán lǐ tīngzhe gē ne.) He was listening to music in the park.
我们正在思考着这件事。(Tā zài gōngyuán lǐ tīngzhe gē ne.) We are thinking about this."
[{2023-05-20 retrieved} https://www.digmandarin.com/commonly-used-chinese-grammar-particles.html]

Zhon_verb_auxi.aspect-particle

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2025-07-10}
"### **Aspect Particles (动态助词) in Chinese**
Aspect particles (also called **"aspect markers"**) are function words in Chinese that indicate the **temporal state or completion of an action**. Unlike tense (past/present/future), which marks when an action occurs, **aspect** focuses on **how the action unfolds in time**—whether it’s completed, ongoing, or experienced.
Chinese relies heavily on aspect particles (rather than verb conjugations) to express these nuances.
---
### **Key Aspect Particles in Chinese**
| Particle | Function | Example | Meaning |
|----------|----------|---------|---------|
| **了 (le)** | **Completed action** or **change of state** | 我吃饭**了**。 | "I **have eaten**." (action done) |
| | | 下雨**了**。 | "It **has started** raining." (change) |
| **过 (guo)** | **Past experience** (ever done something) | 我去**过**北京。 | "I **have been** to Beijing." |
| **着 (zhe)** | **Ongoing state** or **continuous action** | 门开**着**。 | "The door **is open**." |
| | | 她笑**着**说话。 | "She spoke **while smiling**." |
| **在 (zài) / 正在 (zhèngzài)** | **Progressive action** (currently happening) | 我**在**吃饭。 | "I **am eating**." |
---
### **Special Notes on 了 (le)**
The particle **了** is particularly complex because it has **two main uses**:
1. **Verb-complement 了 (action completed)**
- 我买**了**一本书。 ("I bought a book.")
2. **Sentence-final 了 (change of state)**
- 下雨**了**。 ("It started raining.")
- 我不喝酒**了**。 ("I don’t drink anymore.")
In your sentence (**"我以后不喝酒了"**), **了** is **sentence-final**, signaling that the speaker’s behavior **has changed** (they used to drink, but now they won’t).
---
### **Aspect Particles vs. Tense**
- **English** uses verb conjugations (*-ed, -ing*) to show tense.
- **Chinese** uses word order, adverbs (昨天, 明天), and **aspect particles** to indicate time.
Example:
- 昨天我吃**了**饭。 ("Yesterday, I ate.") – **了** confirms completion.
- 明天我要吃饭。 ("Tomorrow, I will eat.") – No particle needed for future.
---
### **Conclusion**
Aspect particles are **essential** in Chinese grammar to express **how an action relates to time** (completed, ongoing, experienced). Mastering them helps sound more natural in speech and writing.
Would you like more examples or a comparison with modal particles (吗, 吧, 呢)?"
[{2025-07-10 retrieved} https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/80f36999-88b4-4130-8720-1b3fc804a059]

name::
* McsEngl.aspect-particle--of-Zhon_verb_auxi,
* McsEngl.Zhon_verb_auxi.aspect-particle,

Zhon_verb_auxi.modal-particle

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2025-07-10}
"### **Modal Particles (语气助词) in Chinese**
Modal particles (**语气助词**, *yǔqì zhùcí*) are small words added at the **end of sentences** to convey **mood, attitude, or emphasis**. Unlike aspect particles (了, 过, 着), which indicate time-related states, modal particles **do not change the core meaning** of a sentence but instead add **emotional tone, politeness, or rhetorical force**.
They are **extremely common** in spoken Chinese and make speech sound more natural.
---
## **Common Modal Particles & Their Functions**
| Particle | Function | Example | Translation |
|----------|----------|---------|-------------|
| **吗 (ma)** | Turns a statement into a **yes-no question** | 你喜欢他**吗**？ | "Do you like him?" |
| **呢 (ne)** | Softens a question, adds curiosity, or continues a topic | 你在做什么**呢**？ | "What are you doing?" |
| | Also used in **contrastive questions** | 我很好，你**呢**？ | "I'm fine, and you?" |
| **吧 (ba)** | Suggests **guessing, suggestion, or seeking agreement** | 我们走**吧**！ | "Let's go!" |
| | | 他是老师**吧**？ | "He's a teacher, right?" |
| **啊 (a)** | Expresses **emphasis, surprise, or emotion** | 你好**啊**！ | "Hey, hello!" |
| | Can soften a statement or exclamation | 真漂亮**啊**！ | "So beautiful!" |
| **的 (de)** | Adds **certainty or emphasis** (often with 是) | 他会来**的**。 | "He **will** come." |
| **了 (le)** | Indicates **a new situation or change** (not aspect!) | 我明白**了**。 | "Now I understand." |
| **嘛 (ma)** | Implies **obviousness or persuasion** | 这很简单**嘛**！ | "It's so simple!" |
---
### **Key Differences Between Modal and Aspect Particles**
| Feature | Modal Particles | Aspect Particles |
|---------|----------------|----------------|
| **Position** | Usually at the **end** of a sentence | Can be **after the verb** or at the end |
| **Function** | Express **mood, attitude, questions** | Show **action completion, experience, or continuation** |
| **Example** | 你好**吗**？ ("Are you okay?") | 我吃**了**。 ("I ate.") |
---
### **Nuances in Usage**
1. **吗 (ma) vs. 呢 (ne) in Questions**
- **吗** → Direct yes-no questions (你喜欢咖啡**吗**？)
- **呢** → Follow-up or open-ended questions (你呢？ / 他在哪儿呢？)
2. **吧 (ba) for Suggestions & Guessing**
- 我们吃饭**吧**！ ("Let's eat!")
- 这是你的书**吧**？ ("This is your book, right?")
3. **啊 (a) for Emotional Tone**
- 快走**啊**！ ("Hurry up!")
- 太好了**啊**！ ("That's great!")
4. **的 (de) for Strong Assertion**
- 他一定会来**的**。 ("He will definitely come.")
---
### **Why Are Modal Particles Important?**
- Make speech sound **natural and fluent**.
- Convey **politeness, hesitation, or emphasis**.
- Turn statements into **questions or suggestions** without changing word order.
**Example Without vs. With Modal Particle:**
- 你去。 ("You go.") → Neutral command.
- 你去**吧**。 ("Go ahead.") → Softer, suggesting.
- 你去**吗**？ ("Are you going?") → Question.
- 你去**啊**？ ("You're going?") → Surprise.
---
### **Conclusion**
Modal particles are **essential for natural-sounding Chinese**, especially in conversation. They don’t change the core meaning but add **tone, mood, and subtlety**.
Would you like a deeper breakdown of a specific particle (e.g., how 呢 changes meaning in different contexts)?"
[{2025-07-10 retrieved} https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/80f36999-88b4-4130-8720-1b3fc804a059]

omission of Zhon_verb

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2026-07-19}

· _sntxZhon: 黄河 在 中国。 :: _sntxSubj:[Huánghé] _sntxSpace:[(zài) zhōngguó]。 != [Yellow river] [(in) China]

"In Chinese grammar, the **omission (or ellipsis) of verbs** is a common and natural phenomenon, but it is **highly context-dependent**. Unlike in English, where a verb is almost always required to form a complete sentence, Chinese allows verb omission to avoid repetition, streamline sentences, or maintain conversational flow.
Here is a comprehensive breakdown of when, how, and why Chinese omits verbs.
---
### 1. Omission of the Main Verb in Parallel Structures
This is the most common and grammatically "standard" omission. When two clauses share the same verb, the verb in the second clause is often dropped to avoid redundancy.
- **Example:**
- Full: 我**喝**咖啡，他**喝**茶。(Wǒ hē kāfēi, tā hē chá. - I drink coffee, he drinks tea.)
- Omitted: 我**喝**咖啡，他茶。(Wǒ hē kāfēi, tā chá. - I drink coffee, he [drinks] tea.)
- **Example with a prepositional verb (coverb):**
- Full: 我**坐**飞机去北京，他**坐**火车去北京。
- Omitted: 我**坐**飞机去北京，他火车去北京。(I go to Beijing by plane, he [goes] by train.)
---
### 2. Omission in "Topic-Comment" Structures
Chinese is a topic-prominent language. The topic is placed at the beginning, and the comment follows. If the verb is easily inferred from the topic, it is often omitted.
- **Example:** 你饭吃了吗？(Nǐ fàn chī le ma? - Literally: "You meal eat yet?")
- In the answer, the verb is often dropped entirely: **吃了** (Chī le - Ate) or even just **了** in casual speech.
- More relevantly, in descriptive sentences: 那个房间**三扇窗户**。(Nà ge fángjiān sān shàn chuānghu. - That room [has] three windows.) The verb "has" (有) is omitted because the topic (room) makes the existence clear.
---
### 3. Omission of the Verb in "Yes/No" A-not-A Questions
In casual speech, the verb in an A-not-A question can be dropped, leaving only the affirmative/negative particles.
- **Full:** 你**要**不要喝茶？(Nǐ yào bú yào hē chá? - Do you want to drink tea?)
- **Omitted:** 你**要**不要茶？(Nǐ yào bú yào chá? - Do you want [to drink] tea?) – Here, the verb "喝" (drink) is omitted because the object "茶" (tea) implies the action.
---
### 4. Omission After Modal Verbs (Auxiliary Verbs)
When a modal verb (能 *néng* - can, 会 *huì* - will/know how, 想 *xiǎng* - want) is used, the main action verb is frequently omitted if it is clear from the context.
- **Question:** 你会游泳吗？(Nǐ huì yóuyǒng ma? - Do you know how to swim?)
- **Answer:** 我会。(Wǒ huì. - I know how [to swim].) – The verb 游泳 is dropped entirely.
---
### 5. Omission in "Resultative Complements" and Directional Complements
When a verb is paired with a complement (indicating result or direction), the main verb can sometimes be dropped in imperative or casual sentences, leaving only the complement to imply the action.
- **Full:** 你**走**进来吧。(Nǐ zǒu jìnlái ba. - Walk in.)
- **Omitted (casual):** 你进来吧。(Nǐ jìnlái ba. - Come in.) – The specific manner of movement (走) is omitted, leaving only the directional verb (进来).
---
### 6. Omission of the Copula "是" (shì - to be)
Unlike English, the copula **是** is **not** used to link a subject to an adjective (predicative adjectives). However, it is also frequently omitted when linking a subject to a noun phrase in casual or elliptical speech.
- **Full:** 我**是**中国人。(Wǒ shì Zhōngguó rén. - I am Chinese.)
- **Omitted (headlines/casual):** 你**是**笨蛋！(Nǐ shì bèndàn! - You are an idiot!) → In very rapid speech, this can drop to 你笨蛋！, though this is colloquial and grammatically informal.
---
### 7. Conversational Ellipsis (Dialogue)
In back-and-forth dialogue, verbs are omitted to make responses snappy.
- **A:** 你去超市吗？(Nǐ qù chāoshì ma? - Are you going to the supermarket?)
- **B:** 去。(Qù. - [I'm] going.)
- **B (if not going):** 不。(Bù. - [I'm] not [going].) – The verb and object are entirely dropped.
---
### Important Grammar Rules to Remember
| Rule | OK to Omit? | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Omit repeated verbs in parallel clauses** | ✅ Yes (and encouraged) | 我唱歌，他跳舞。(I sing, he dances.) – The verb for "he" is omitted if it matches. |
| **Omit the main verb after a modal** | ✅ Yes | 你能吗？(Can you [do it]?) |
| **Omit the verb before an object in casual questions** | ✅ Yes | 你喝水吗？→ 你水吗？(Do you want water?) – Only in very casual speech. |
| **Omit the verb when it's the only word in a sentence** | ✅ Yes | 走！(Go!) / 吃！(Eat!) |
| **Omit the verb "有" (yǒu - to have) in existential sentences** | ❌ **Rarely** | 房间里**有**桌子。(There is a table in the room.) – You cannot drop 有 here; it would become ungrammatical. |
| **Omit the verb when the object is a long clause** | ❌ No | 我**知道**他来了。(I know he came.) – You cannot drop 知道. |
---
### The Golden Rule of Verb Omission
**You can only omit a verb in Chinese if the listener can 100% deduce what the verb is from the immediate context, the shared knowledge between speakers, or the grammatical structure of the preceding clause.**
If omitting the verb creates ambiguity about *who* is doing *what* to *whom*, the verb must remain. For example, you cannot omit the verb in "我打他" (I hit him), because omitting it ("我他") is nonsensical.
---
### A Critical Warning: Do NOT omit the verb "有" (to have/exist)
This is the most common mistake learners make.
- ❌ Incorrect: 教室三个学生。(Jiàoshì sān ge xuésheng. - Classroom three students.)
- ✅ Correct: 教室**有**三个学生。(Jiàoshì yǒu sān ge xuésheng. - There are three students in the classroom.)
The verb 有 is essential for expressing existence and possession and **cannot** be omitted in standard grammar."
[{2026-07-19 retrieved} https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/0d97bcad-a128-4208-bd14-06a8ee534ff3]

Zhon_verb.separable

description::
"certain verbs in Chinese are normally linked together with its own particular Object, and the “Verb + its Object” is usually seen as one single verb unit."
[{2021-10-16 retrieved} http://www.chinese-grammar.com/beginner/verb-object.html]
===
"Separable verbs are "verb-object phrases." They consist of two characters: the first is the verb, and the second is the object. Very often, these two will appear together, seemingly acting as a single verb, as in 吃饭, "to eat," 见面, "to meet," or 睡觉, "to sleep." But the two can also separate, and the verb can also be used without the object."
[{2021-10-16 retrieved} https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/Separable_verb]

* chán-缠 – 1. to coil 把绳子缠起来。(Wind up the rope.) 2. to tangle 线已缠在一起。 (The thread is tangled.) 3. to entangle; to pester 别缠我。(Leave me alone.)
* chán-馋 – 1. to use food to tempt someone 别用羊肉串儿馋我。(Don’t use lamb shish kebabs to tempt me.) 2. to have a gluttonous craving 我馋了。(I wanna pig out.)
* chéng-乘 – 1. to board 他乘的是384航班。(He boarded flight 384.) 2. to multiply 2乘 3等于6。(Two times three is six.)
* chí-持 – 1. to hold 2. to manage
* chù-怵 – 1. to be unwilling to do something because it’s too challenging 2. to be scared of 我什么人都不怵。(I’m not scared of anyone.)
* chā-插 – 1. to insert 2. to stab 3. to fuck
* chāo-抄 – 1. to copy 不要炒你同学的作业。(Don’t copy your classmates’ work.) 2. to use (in different collocations) 抄近路。(Take a shortcut.) 抄家伙。(Take your weapons out.)
* chēng-撑 – 1. to open (umbrella, parasol, etc) 把它撑开。(Open it up.) 2. to be full/stuffed 我撑死了。(I’m stuffed.) 3. to put up with我快撑不住了。(I can’t take it anymore.)
* chě-扯 – 1. to pull on; to yank; to tug 他扯了扯我的衣角。(He tugged at my clothes.) 2. to talk shit 别扯了。(Stop talking bullshit.)
* chōng-冲 – 1. rinse 2. flush 3. recharge 4. charge/collide 5. develop a film
* chōu-抽 – 1. to take out 2. to smoke 3. to find (time) 4. to release 5. to shrink/contract 6. to pump out
* chǎo-吵 – to quarrel; to argue; to be noisy 别吵啦。(Don’t argue.)
* chǎo-炒 – 1. stir-fry 2. to dismiss; to fire; to sack 3. to invest heavily and make prices go up 去年的澳洲房价高涨当地媒体说都是外国投资者炒起来。(The media have said that the reason house prices in Australia went up last year was due to overseas buyers flooding the market.)
* cuī-催 – to urge
* cuō-搓 – 1. to rub 2. to do something 咱们搓一顿吧。(Let’s grab a bite to eat.) 他们 正在搓麻将。(They’re playing mahjong.)
* cáng-藏 – 1. to hide something or someone; to harbour 2. to store
* cì-刺 – 1. to stab 2. to sting
* cǎi-踩 – 1. to step on 2. to make a simple comment on a blog/post
* diào-掉 – 1. to lose 2. to drop
* diū-丢 – 1. to lose 2. to throw 3. to litter
* diǎn-点 – 1. to point; to poke 2. to mention 3. order (food, drinks, etc)
* diǎo-鸟 – 1. to talk to somebody 他不鸟我。(He’s not talking to me.)
* duǒ-躲 – 1. to hide 2. to avoid 3. to dodge 他躲过了子弹。(He dodged a bullet.) 我们 躲过了一场灾难。(We managed to escape from the disaster.)
* dài-带 – 1. to carry 2. to lead 3. to bring up
* dé-得 – 1. to receive 2. to contract an illness 3. to have had enough, e.g. 得了吧！(Stop it!) 4. děi – have to
* dìng-订 – 1. to order 2. to book; to reserve
* dú-读 – 1. to read 2. to study, e.g. 念书 and 读书.
* dēng-蹬 – 1. to step 2. to dump
* dūn-蹲 – 1. to squat 2. to stay at home
* dǎ-打 – 1. to hit 2. to call 3. to play 4. many additional meanings, especially in compounds
* dǎo-倒 – 1. to fall down 2. -_- (Internet slang)
* dǐng-顶 – 1. to carry on the head 2. to approve; to support (Internet slang)
* fèi-废 – 1. to injury someone badly把他废了。(I disabled him.) 2. to be ruined beyond repair车废了。(The car is beyond repair.) 3. to be useless他人废了。(He’s useless.)
* féng-逢 – to meet 他雅思得了四个7，高兴极了，逢人便说。(He got four 7s for his IELTS and was so happy that he told every one he met.)
* fú-服 – to give in好啦，我服了。 (Okay, I give in.)
* fú-浮 – 1. to float 2. to drift (usually through life)
* fā-发 – 1. to send 2. to make a fortune
* fān-翻 – 1. to turn over 2. to translate

* guā-刮 – 1. to scrape 2. to shave 3. to scrub

* gài-盖 – 1. to cover 妈妈会给你盖好的。(Mum will tuck you in.) 太冷了，你要盖好 被子。(It’s freezing – stay under the doona.) 2. to surpass; to exceed 在《水浒传》 中，宋江的功劳盖了晁盖。 (In Water Margin Song Jiang’s contribution exceeded that of Chao Gai.)

* gǎn-赶 – 1. to be equally matched他的英语不赶你好。(His English is no match for yours.) 2. to push or force someone to leave 不用赶，我自己会走！ (You don’t have to kick me out, I’ll leave on my own accord!)
* huǐ-毁 – to ruin 他毁了我们的婚姻。(He ruined our marriage.)
* huǒ-火 – (noun: fire) 1. to be famous 他火得厉害。(He’s very famous.) 2. to get angry 他火大了。(He flared up.)
* hài-害 – 1. to put in harm’s way; to jeopardise 别害他。(Don’t put him in harm’s way.) 2. to cause something bad to happen 你没来，害得我等了一个小时。(I had to wait a whole hour because you didn’t show up.)
* hàn-汗 – 1. to sweat 2. -_- (Internet slang)
* hán-含 – 1. to contain 2. to keep/have in the mouth
* hùn-混 1. to be busy doing something 你混得怎么样？(What you been up to lately?) 2. to drift (usually through life) 最近瞎混。(Just been stuffin’ around.) 他每天不工作 ，就在家混日子。(He never works, just bums around at home.)

* jiá-夹 – 1. fold 2. slam

* jiǎo-缴 – 1. to pay money 2. to hand in

* kào-靠 – 1. to rely on 2. to fuck

* lí-离 – to divorce 我们俩离了。(We’re divorced.)

* 涮 shuàn – 1. to rinse 2. to make fun of (old-fashioned) 他涮咱们呢，别信他的话。 (He’s making fun of us, don’t believe what he says.)
* 侃 kǎn – to talk a lot 他这个人很能侃。(He sure talks a lot.)
* 砍 kǎn – 1. to cut down 2. to cut 他砍到我手了！(He cut my hand!)
* 挟 xié – 1. hold under one’s arm (夹住) 2. coerce (挟制) 3. harbour (心怀)
* 眯 mī – 1. squint 2. take a nap
* 脱 tuō – 1. to take off clothing 2. to get away with 如果我们被抓了，你也脱不了关 系。(If we get caught, there’s no way you can get out of it.)
* 掖 yē – 1. to support somebody by one’s arm; to tuck in; to thrust in between 2. help; assist
* 抱 bào – 1. carry in one’s arms 2. adopt; hold 3. cherish 4. hang out 5. hatch
* 爆 bào – 1. to explode 2. to fuck 我把他菊花爆了。(I fucked him up the arse.)
* 系 jì – 1. to tie up; to fasten 请把你的安全带系上。(Please put your seat belt on.) 2. xì to be 毛泽东系湖南人。(Mao Zedong is from Hunan.)
* 抽 chōu – 1. to take out 2. to smoke 3. to find (time) 4. to release 5. to shrink/contract 6. to pump out
* 封 fēng – to seal 把那个窗户封死。(Seal the window up.)
* 聚 jù – 1. to gather; to congregate 我们今天在学校聚一聚。(We met up at school today.)
* 奔 bèn – to run in a hurry 他刚奔出去。(He just rushed out.)
* 圆 yuán – 1. to make round 2. to justify; to explain 她的故事圆不上了。(Her story is inexplicable.) 3. to make a reality (e.g. a dream) 他圆了她的梦。(She made her dream come true.)
* 守 shǒu – 1. to guard 2. to be with for a long time 她守着残疾的丈夫过了二十年。 (She stayed by her disabled husband’s side for 20 years.)
* 受 shòu – 1. to tolerate 我受不了。(I can’t take it anymore.) 2. to enjoy 这部电影很 受欢迎。(This movie is very popular [lit. “enjoys popularity].) 偶爸妈很受爱戴。 (Obama has garnered much support [lit. “enjoys love and support”].) 观音菩萨极其 灵验，广受香火。(The Goddess of Mercy answers people’s prayers and is widely worshipped [lit. “widely enjoys incense”].)
* 爬 pá – 1. to climb 2. to crawl
* 炒 chǎo – 1. stir-fry 2. to dismiss; to fire; to sack 3. to invest heavily and make prices go up 去年的澳洲房价高涨当地媒体说都是外国投资者炒起来。(The media have said that the reason house prices in Australia went up last year was due to overseas buyers flooding the market.)
* 怨 yuàn – to blame
* 惹 rě – to provoke; to stir up 谁惹起这件事？(Who started it?) 他总喜欢惹人注意。 (He likes to attract attention.) 别惹乱子。(Don’t stir up trouble.) 他这个人很惹人厌 。(He’s a nuisance.)
* 招 zhāo – 1. to beckon 2. to provoke; to stir up 3. to recruit
* 驳 bó – to refute 我驳不倒他。(I can’t prove him wrong.)
* 补 bǔ – 1. to supplement 2. to mend; to patch up; to repair
* 躲 duǒ – 1. to hide 2. to avoid 3. to dodge 他躲过了子弹。(He dodged a bullet.) 我们 躲过了一场灾难。(We managed to escape from the disaster.)
* 藏 cáng – 1. to hide something or someone; to harbour 2. to store
* 缴 jiǎo – 1. to pay money 2. to hand in
* 订 dìng – 1. to order 2. to book; to reserve
* 丢 diū – 1. to lose 2. to throw 3. to litter
* 许 xǔ – 1. to allow; to permit 2. to promise
* 漏 lòu – 1. to leak 2. to reveal; to leak information
* 勾 gōu – 1. to seduce 2. to evoke 他说的话勾起了我的回忆。(What he said brought back some memories.) 3. to tick 把它勾掉。(Tick it off.)
* 抢 qiǎng – 1. to mug; to steal 他抢了我钱包。(He mugged me and took my wallet.) 2. to rob 他抢了银行。(He robbed the bank.) 3. to scramble for; to vie for; to rush for 我 们抢着做刷碗。(We both insisted on washing the dishes.) 4. to yank; to grab
* 挣 zhēng 1. to scramble for; to vie for; to rush for 2. to open 把袋子挣开。(Open your bag.) – zhèng to earn money 我今天挣了30。(Today I earned thirty bucks.)
* 免 miǎn – 1. to avoid 2. to exempt; to excuse
* 欠 qiàn – 1. to owe 2. to lack 他做事欠妥当。(He doesn’t do things properly.) 3. to move forward slightly (to adjust the position of one’s body)
* 戒 jiè – to abstain from; give up; to quit 他戒烟了。(He quit smoking.) 她戒酒了。 (She gave up drinking.)
* 养 yǎng – 1. to bring up; to cultivate; to raise 他养花，养狗，也养鱼，但还没养过 孩子。(He cultivates flowers, raises dogs and he’s even got some fish, but he’s never brought up any children.) 2. to support 父母赚钱养你不容易。(It’s not easy for your parents to earn enough money to support you.)
* 领 lǐng – 1. to lead; to guide 2. to receive 每个月你领了多少工资？(How much salary do you get each month?)
* 宰 zǎi – 1. to slaughter; to butcher 2. to be ripped off 你被宰了。(You were ripped off.)
* 离 lí – to divorce 我们俩离了。(We’re divorced.)
* 架 jià – to take someone away forcibly 把他架出去。(Kick him out.)
* 抓 zhuā – 1. to scratch 2. to grab 3. to grope; to fondle 他抓了她的胸。(He groped her breasts.) 4. to catch 5. to arrest
* 编 biān – 1. to weave 2. to make a list 3. to edit
* 持 chí – 1. to hold 2. to manage
* 传 chuán – 1. to pass on 2. to spread 3. to transmit
* 带 dài – 1. to carry 2. to lead 3. to bring up
* 告 gào – 1. to tell 2. to announce 3. to sue
* 集 jí – 1. to collect 2. to gather
* 理 lǐ – 1. to take notice of 2. to manage 3. to realise
* 连 lián – 1. to join 2. continue
* 求 qiú – 1. to beg for 2. to seek
* 容 róng – 1. to tolerate 2. to allow
* 赛 sài – 1. to race 2. to rival
* 砸 zá – to smash 我用锤子砸他的头。(I smashed his head in with a hammer.)
* 追 zhuī – 1. to chase 2. to reminisce 3. to act retroactively
* 接 jiē – 1. to pick up someone 今天晚上下班我来接你。(I’ll pick you up after work this evening.) 2. to answer; to continue talking 你倒是往下接啊！ (What are you waiting for? Keep going.)
* 考 kǎo – to test oneself 这个你还真考不倒我！(I can answer this question!)
* 托 tuō – to hold in the palm 麻烦你过来帮我托一下，好吗？ (Can you come over here and hold this for me please?)
* 扇 shān – 1. to slap one’s face 我当时真想扇他一巴掌。(At that time I really wanted to slap him in the face.) 2. to fan 你能不能别扇了？怪闹心的！ (Can you please just stop using your fan for a sec? It’s so annoying!)
* 拍 pāi – 1. to take a photo of someone 别拍，别拍，我都不好意思了！ (Please don’t take photo of me! I’m a bit shy!) 2. to pat 他走了过去，拍了拍我。(He came over and gave me a pat on the shoulder.) 我的小狗喜欢我拍他。(My doggie likes it when I pat him.)
* 赶 gǎn – 1. to be equally matched他的英语不赶你好。(His English is no match for yours.) 2. to push or force someone to leave 不用赶，我自己会走！ (You don’t have to kick me out, I’ll leave on my own accord!)
* 扯 chě – 1. to pull on; to yank; to tug 他扯了扯我的衣角。(He tugged at my clothes.) 2. to talk shit 别扯了。(Stop talking bullshit.)
* 缠 chán – 1. to coil 把绳子缠起来。(Wind up the rope.) 2. to tangle 线已缠在一起。 (The thread is tangled.) 3. to entangle; to pester 别缠我。(Leave me alone.)
* 馋 chán – 1. to use food to tempt someone 别用羊肉串儿馋我。(Don’t use lamb shish kebabs to tempt me.) 2. to have a gluttonous craving 我馋了。(I wanna pig out.)
[{2021-10-16 retrieved} https://qingdaoamerasia.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/A-Detailed-Guide-to-One-Character-Verbs-in-Mandarin.pdf]

× Mcsh-creation: {2026-07-09}
· 远离 (yuǎnlí), means "to stay away from," "to keep far from," or "to be far away from." It's a verb made up of 远 (yuǎn - far) + 离 (lí - to leave/from). It's commonly used in both formal and informal contexts, often in advice, warnings, or descriptive statements.

Zhon_verb.regularNo

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2026-06-11}
"In standard Mandarin Chinese, the concept of "irregular verbs" as found in Indo-European languages (e.g., go/went/gone in English) does not exist. Chinese verbs do not conjugate for tense, person, number, or aspect. However, there are a few special cases that are sometimes loosely referred to as "irregular" in pedagogical contexts:
1. **The verb 去 (qù – to go)** – When used in directional complements, its form can change in certain colloquial contractions, e.g., 回去 (huíqù) → 回 (huí) + 去 (qù) sometimes contracts in speech, but not a true irregularity.
2. **The verb 有 (yǒu – to have)** – Its negative form is 没有 (méiyǒu), not *不有 (bù yǒu), which is a fixed suppletive pattern.
3. **The copula 是 (shì – to be)** – No irregular conjugation, but its negative is 不是 (bù shì) following standard negation rules.
4. **Modal verbs like 能 (néng – can)** – Negation uses 不 (bù) instead of 没 (méi), but this is consistent across modals, not irregular.
5. **Reduplication patterns** – Some verbs change tone or reduce the second syllable (e.g., 看看 kànkan, not kànkàn), which is a regular phonological rule, not grammatical irregularity.
In summary: **Chinese has no irregular verbs in the grammatical sense**. All verbs maintain a single invariant form, with aspect and mood expressed via separate particles (了, 过, 着, 在) following regular rules. The term "irregular" is only applicable if you compare to languages with verb conjugation."
[{2026-06-11 retrieved} https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/2b86d6f7-f3f0-4293-ad32-e625cc510298]

Zhon_conj.de-地

description::

=== _syntaxZhon: Adje + 地 + Verb
· _sntxZhon: 慢慢地 走 :: _sntxManner:[[mànmàn](de)] _sntxVerb:{zǒu}. != slowly walk.
· _sntxZhon: 生气 地 说 :: _sntxManner:[shēngqì (de)] _sntxVerb:{shuō} != angrily say
"$ 请慢慢地说。 vs 请慢慢说。in english:
The difference is purely one of **register and style** — the meaning is identical: *"Please speak slowly."*
**请慢慢地说。**
- **地 (de)** is the structural particle that explicitly marks an adverb modifying a verb.
- This form is more **formal, written, or grammatically explicit**. It’s what you’d expect in textbooks, formal writing, or when someone is being careful with their grammar.
**请慢慢说。**
- The particle is dropped.
- This is more **colloquial, spoken, and natural** in everyday conversation. Native speakers omit this "地" all the time in casual speech because it flows more smoothly.
**In short:**
- **慢慢地说** = formal / written style
- **慢慢说** = casual / spoken style
Both are perfectly correct. If you’re speaking naturally with friends, **请慢慢说** sounds more relaxed and native. If you’re writing an essay or a formal letter, **请慢慢地说** looks more polished."
[{2026-07-30 retrieved} https://www.kimi.com/chat/19fb2816-66a2-8620-8000-094ba6952669?chat_enter_method=new_chat]

=== _syntaxZhon: Adve + 地 + Adje
· _sntxZhon: 特别地珍贵 :: tèbié de zhēnguì != particularly precious

===
"Even native Chinese speakers sometimes misuse 的 and 地, both of which can be structural particles. When used as a structural particle, 地 is often placed after adjectives and adverbs to serve as an adverbial marker.
Adjective / Adverb + 地 + Verb phrase / Adjective"
[{2023-05-20 retrieved} https://www.digmandarin.com/commonly-used-chinese-grammar-particles.html]

Zhon_conj.hé-和!=rltnAddition

description::

× mind-relation: rltnAddition,
"One of the most common English words is the word “and,” which we use to connect nouns, verbs, phrases and sentences. “And” is often translated to “和(hé)” in Chinese. However, in Chinese, you cannot use “和” to connect sentences – the result would sound very awkward!
we can use “和” to connect nouns, verbs, and short non-sentence phrases.
· _sntxZhon: 我有两个哥哥和一个妹妹。 :: Wǒ yǒu liǎng gè gēgē hé yīgè mèimei. != I have two older brothers and a younger sister.
· _sntxZhon: 他喜欢游泳和打篮球。 :: Tā _sntxVerb:{xǐhuān} _sntxSbjc:[[yóuyǒng] (hé) [dǎ lánqiú]]. != He likes swimming and playing basketball."
[{2023-05-21 retrieved} https://www.digmandarin.com/top-20-common-mistakes-chinese-learners-make.html]

· _sntxZhon: 你 和 我 :: nǐ hé wǒ != you and I

· Postposition (Time): Means "after". In Chinese, time words like 后 (after), 前 (before), 时 (when) come after the noun/verb they modify. Together, 发射后 forms a temporal adverbial phrase meaning "after launch" / "after the launch". [DeepSeek]

· _sntxZhon: 我 再三考虑后 决定 辞职。 :: Wǒ _sntxTime:[zài sān kǎolǜ (hòu)] _sntxVerb:{juédìng} cízhí.!= I decided to resign after considering it over and over. != 后 (hòu) — Noun/Postposition: "after, behind, later" [DeepSeek]

× Mcsh-creation: {2026-07-08}
· 无 (wú) — which means "without", "not have", "none", or "nothing".

Zhon_conj.postposition

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2026-07-14}

"Chinese postpositions are a fascinating part of the language's grammar. They are words that come **after** a noun or noun phrase to indicate its relationship to other parts of the sentence, often expressing location, time, or abstract concepts.
Think of them as the opposite of prepositions (like "in," "on," or "at" in English), which come **before** the noun.
### 🔍 What They Are and Common Examples
In linguistic terms, postpositions are a subcategory of **adpositions**. While Mandarin has prepositions (like 在 *zài*, 从 *cóng*), it also uses postpositions to add specific spatial, temporal, or abstract meaning to a noun. Here are some of the most common ones:
| Postposition | Pinyin | Meaning & Use | Example | Translation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **里** | lǐ | in, inside | 家里 *jiā lǐ* | in the home |
| **上** | shàng | on, upon; in (abstract) | 理论上 *lǐlùn shàng* | in theory |
| **下** | xià | under, below; under (circumstances) | 树 *shù xià* | under the tree |
| **前** | qián | in front of; before | 考试 *kǎoshì qián* | before the exam |
| **后 / 以后** | hòu / yǐhòu | behind; after | 三天后 *sān tiān hòu* | three days later |
| **外** | wài | outside; beyond | 城 *chéng wài* | outside the city |
| **之间** | zhījiān | between, among | 我们之间 *wǒmen zhījiān* | between us |
| **旁边** | pángbiān | beside, next to | 篝火旁边 *gōuhuǒ pángbiān* | beside the bonfire |
| **以来** | yǐlái | since | 他到来以来 *tā dàolái yǐlái* | since his arrival (since he came) |
### 🧠 A Key Concept: Circumpositions
A really common and important structure in Mandarin is the **circumposition**. This is when a noun is "bracketed" by both a preposition **and** a postposition, working together to express a meaning.
- **Structure**: Preposition + Noun + Postposition
- **Example**: 从 + 桌子 + 上 (*cóng + zhuōzi + shàng) = from + table + on = **from on the table**.
In this construction, the preposition (like 从 *cóng*) often indicates a **path or direction**, while the postposition (like 上 *shàng*) indicates a specific **place or location**. A classic case is the preposition 在 (*zài*), which is used to check the grammatical case of the postpositional phrase, making phrases like 在...上 (*zài...shàng* - "on") or 在...里 (*zài...lǐ* - "in") possible.
### 📝 How to Use Them
1. **Postpositions Follow the Noun**: They always come immediately after the noun they modify, with nothing in between.
2. **Phrases Can Be Subjects**: Unlike prepositional phrases, a phrase ending with a postposition (a PostP) can often serve as the subject of a sentence. For example, "桌子上有书" (Zhuōzi shàng yǒu shū) literally means "Table-on has books," or "There are books on the table".
3. **Postpositions Are Not Nouns**: This is a key distinction. Words like 上 (*shàng*) and 里 (*lǐ*) are grammatical particles, not full nouns like 上面 (*shàngmiàn* - "top side"). You can say 理论上 (*lǐlùn shàng* - "in theory"), but you **cannot** say 理论上面 (*lǐlùn shàngmiàn*), which would mean "the top side of the theory" and is ungrammatical.
Mandarin's postpositions are a great example of how the language creates meaning through word order and structure. They're a key part of making expressions precise, especially when talking about time, place, and abstract ideas."
[{2026-07-14 retrieved} https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/7a100232-73e9-402b-9988-cb7caa4736a0]

===
"In Chinese grammar, "postpositions" fall into two distinct categories: **locative postpositions** (方位后置词) that follow nouns to indicate spatial/temporal relationships, and **aspectual particles** (动态助词) that follow verbs to indicate how an action relates to time. Here's a comprehensive overview.
---
## 1. Locative Postpositions (方位后置词)
These function similarly to English prepositions like "in," "on," or "under," but they appear **after** the noun they modify, forming a "Postpositional Phrase" (PostP).
### Common Locative Postpositions
| Postposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **上** (shàng) | on, above | 桌子上 (zhuōzi shàng) — on the table |
| **下** (xià) | under, below | 椅子下 (yǐzi xià) — under the chair |
| **里** (lǐ) | in, inside | 房间里 (fángjiān lǐ) — in the room |
| **内** (nèi) | inside, within | 三天内 (sān tiān nèi) — within three days |
| **外** (wài) | outside, beyond | 学校外 (xuéxiào wài) — outside the school |
| **前** (qián) | in front of; before | 门前 (mén qián) — in front of the door |
| **后** (hòu) | behind; after | 饭后 (fàn hòu) — after the meal |
| **中** (zhōng) | amidst, in the middle of | 人群中 (rénqún zhōng) — in the crowd |
| **旁** (páng) | next to, beside | 窗户旁 (chuānghu páng) — beside the window |
| **间** (jiān) | between | 两棵树间 (liǎng kē shù jiān) — between two trees |
### Compound/Disyllabic Forms
Mandarin often uses two-syllable variants for more natural speech:
- **上面** (shàngmiàn) — on top of
- **下边** (xiàbiān) — underneath
- **里面** (lǐmiàn) — inside
- **前面** (qiánmiàn) — front
- **中间** (zhōngjiān) — middle
- **旁边** (pángbiān) — side
### Temporal Postpositions
These indicate time rather than space:
| Postposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **以前** (yǐqián) | before, ago | 三年以前 (sān nián yǐqián) — three years ago |
| **以后** (yǐhòu) | after | 毕业以后 (bìyè yǐhòu) — after graduation |
| **以来** (yǐlái) | since, during | 长期以来 (chángqī yǐlái) — for a long time |
| **之内** (zhī nèi) | within | 一周之内 (yī zhōu zhī nèi) — within one week |
### Key Syntactic Feature
Unlike nouns, postpositions **cannot** take the subordinator 的 (de) between the noun and the postposition:
- ✅ **桌子上** (zhuōzi shàng) — correct
- ❌ **桌子的上** (zhuōzi de shàng) — incorrect
This distinguishes postpositions from location nouns like 上面 (shàngmiàn), which *can* take 的: 桌子的上面 (zhuōzi de shàngmiàn) — "the top of the table"

---
## 2. Aspectual Particles (动态助词)
These follow verbs to indicate the **aspect** of an action—how it relates to time rather than when it happened.
### 了 (le) — Completion & Change of State
**After a verb:** Marks a completed action.
- 我**吃了**饭。(Wǒ chī le fàn.) — I ate (finished eating).
- 他**买了**一本书。(Tā mǎi le yì běn shū.) — He bought a book.
**At sentence end:** Marks a change of state.
- 下雨**了**。(Xià yǔ le.) — It's raining now (it wasn't before).
- 我饿**了**。(Wǒ è le.) — I'm hungry now.
**Double 了:** Both completion and new state.
- 我**吃了**饭**了**。(Wǒ chī le fàn le.) — I've eaten (finished + new state).
**Negation:** Use 没 (méi) and **drop** 了.
- 我**没**吃饭。(Wǒ méi chī fàn.) — I didn't eat.
### 着 (zhe) — Ongoing Action or State
Indicates an action in progress or a continuous state.
- 他站**着**。(Tā zhàn zhe.) — He is standing.
- 门开**着**。(Mén kāi zhe.) — The door is open.
- 她笑**着**说。(Tā xiào zhe shuō.) — She said while smiling.
**Simultaneous actions:** Verb1 + 着 + Verb2
- 我站**着**吃饭。(Wǒ zhàn zhe chī fàn.) — I eat while standing.
**Negation:** Use 没 + Verb + 着
- 门**没**开**着**。(Mén méi kāi zhe.) — The door isn't open.
### 过 (guo) — Past Experience
Indicates that someone has the experience of doing something, with no focus on when.
- 我去**过**中国。(Wǒ qù guo Zhōngguó.) — I've been to China (before).
- 你吃**过**北京烤鸭吗？(Nǐ chī guo Běijīng kǎoyā ma?) — Have you ever eaten Peking duck?
**Key distinction from 了:**
- 我**去了**中国 = I went to China (specific, recent, completed).
- 我**去过**中国 = I have been to China (experience, time irrelevant).
**Negation:** Use 没 + Verb + 过 (keep 过!)
- 我**没**去**过**中国。(Wǒ méi qù guo Zhōngguó.) — I have never been to China.
---
## Quick Comparison Table
| Particle | Function | Example | Translation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **了** | Completed action | 我吃了 | I ate |
| **了** | Change of state | 下雨了 | It's raining now |
| **着** | Ongoing / continuous | 门开着 | The door is open |
| **过** | Past experience | 我去过 | I've been (before) |
---
## Summary
Chinese postpositions are **post-nominal** (following nouns for location/time) or **post-verbal** (following verbs for aspect). Unlike English prepositions that come before their object, Chinese postpositions consistently appear **after** the element they modify—hence the name. The aspectual particles 了, 着, and 过 are particularly crucial because Chinese verbs do not conjugate for tense; these particles carry the entire temporal and situational load of the sentence."
[{2026-07-20 retrieved} https://www.kimi.com/chat/19f7ff23-d812-856e-8000-094b754654f0?chat_enter_method=shortcut]

Zhon_post'type

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2026-07-28}
"⇒ Chinese postposition are nouns, adverbs, or conjunctions?
This is a nuanced question that gets at the heart of Chinese word classes. The most direct and accurate answer is:
**Chinese postpositions are primarily nouns, with some that can function as adverbs. They are not conjunctions.**
Here is the breakdown.

### 1. Primarily Nouns (Locative Nouns)
The vast majority of what are traditionally called "postpositions" in Chinese are in fact a subclass of nouns known as **locative nouns** (方位词, fāngwèicí).
They do not form a separate syntactic category of "postposition" (like in Japanese or Turkish) but behave syntactically as nouns that are the head of a locative phrase. The structure is typically:
**[NP + 的] + Locative Noun**
- **桌子上** (zhuōzi shàng) - "table-on" = on the table
- **学校里** (xuéxiào lǐ) - "school-in" = in the school
- **三天前** (sān tiān qián) - "three-days-before" = three days ago
- **门外面** (mén wàimiàn) - "door-outside" = outside the door
In this structure, the first noun (e.g., 桌子) is a modifier, and the locative noun (e.g., 上) is the syntactic head. This is why you can often insert the attributive particle 的 (de) with no change in meaning (桌子上面 = 桌子的上面), proving their nominal status. They function as the object of prepositions, the subject or object of a sentence, just like any other noun.

### 2. Can Function as Adverbs (or Adverbials)
Some locative nouns, especially monosyllabic ones, are highly grammaticalized and can function directly as post-verbal adverbials of direction or result. In this position, they have moved from a purely nominal function to a more adverbial one, behaving similarly to verbal complements.
- **走进来** (zǒu jìnlái) - "walk enter-come" = walk in
- **跑过去** (pǎo guòqù) - "run cross-go" = run over there
Here, 进来 (jìnlái) and 过去 (guòqù) are often analyzed as directional complements (a type of adverbial) rather than pure nouns. Some dissyllabic locative nouns can also function as adverbial modifiers without a preceding noun:
- **我们在外面谈。** (Wǒmen zài wàimiàn tán.) - "We at outside talk." Here, 外面 is a locative noun, functioning as the object of the preposition 在. The entire prepositional phrase is the adverbial.
- **外面冷。** (Wàimiàn lěng.) - "Outside is cold." Here, 外面 is the subject, a clear noun function.
- **大家里边坐。** (Dàjiā lǐbian zuò.) - "Everyone inside sit." Here, 里边 functions directly as an adverbial modifier of the verb 坐, without a preposition. This is a more adverbial use.
So, a single word like 外面 (wàimiàn) can be a noun (as a subject) or part of an adverbial phrase, but it does not fundamentally change its lexical category; it just highlights the fluidity of Chinese word classes.

### 3. Not Conjunctions
Chinese postpositions have no conjunctive function. They do not link clauses or equal syntactic units. A word like 前 (qián, "before") is a locative noun (三天前), not a conjunction meaning "before" in the clausal sense.
To connect clauses, Chinese uses dedicated conjunctions like 以前 (yǐqián) or 在...以前 (zài...yǐqián), which are historically derived from these nouns but are syntactically distinct.
- **他来以前**, 我们得准备好。 (Tā lái yǐqián, wǒmen děi zhǔnbèi hǎo.) - "He come before, we must prepare well." Here, 以前 functions as a postposition to the clause 他来, but the word itself is still a locative noun heading the temporal phrase. It is the whole phrase that functions adverbially, not the word 以前 acting as a conjunction.

### Summary Table
| Function | Syntactic Category | Example | Role of Postposition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Use** | **Noun (Locative Noun)** | 桌子上 (on the table) | Head of a locative noun phrase |
| **Common Use** | **Adverbial** (as part of a phrase or stand-alone) | 外面谈 (talk outside) | Head of an adverbial phrase |
| **Not a Use** | **Conjunction** | (No example) | Chinese postpositions are not conjunctions |
In short, they are a subclass of **nouns** that often take on an **adverbial function** in sentences, which is perfectly consistent with the ability of Chinese nouns to function adverbially when expressing time or location."
[{2026-07-28 retrieved} https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3d089a33-09f9-4104-91f8-3802e90026fd]
